string-array.name: lesson_letters_spot
string-array.item: Arabic is read from right to left.
Most letters join to the next one, so a letter changes shape at the start, middle and end of a word.
Six letters, ا د ذ ر ز و, never join to the letter after them.

string-array.name: lesson_letters_how
string-array.item: Each letter is one consonant. The vowels are the small marks above and below it.
بِسۡمِ is three letters joined together: ب, س and م.

string-array.name: lesson_short_vowels_spot
string-array.item: Fatḥa: a small slanted line above the letter (بَ).
Kasra: the same line below the letter (بِ).
Ḍamma: a small curl like a wāw above the letter (بُ).

string-array.name: lesson_short_vowels_how
string-array.item: Fatḥa sounds like the a in ba, kasra like the i in bi, ḍamma like the u in bu.
Keep them short: one count each.

resources.string: Tanwīn doubles the mark and adds an n sound: ba becomes ban.

string-array.name: lesson_sukun_spot
string-array.item: A small mark like the top of the letter ح, above the letter (بۡ).
The letter has no vowel of its own.

string-array.name: lesson_sukun_how
string-array.item: Say the letter without a vowel, closing the syllable before it.
Don’t add a vowel to it: naʿ, not na-ʿa.

resources.string: A small circle means the letter is not pronounced at all. A letter with sukūn is pronounced, just without a vowel.

string-array.name: lesson_long_vowels_spot
string-array.item: An alif after a fatḥa: بَا
A wāw with no mark after a ḍamma: بُو
A yāʾ with no mark after a kasra: بِي

string-array.name: lesson_long_vowels_how
string-array.item: Stretch the vowel for two counts: bā, bū, bī.
The alif, wāw or yāʾ only lengthens the vowel. It is not a new consonant.

resources.string: A wavy line above the long vowel means: stretch it longer than two counts.

string-array.name: lesson_tanween_spot
string-array.item: A doubled vowel mark on the last letter of a word: بً‎, بٍ‎ or بٌ.
Fatḥatān is usually followed by an alif (بًا). That alif is only read when you stop on the word.

string-array.name: lesson_tanween_how
string-array.item: Say the vowel, then an n: an, in, un.
When you stop on the word, drop the n: -un and -in lose their vowel, and -an becomes ā.
Before some letters the n changes. That is covered by the noon sākinah rules in Tajweed.

resources.string: A single mark is only a short vowel, with no n: ba. Tanwīn doubles it and adds the n: ban.

string-array.name: lesson_hamza_spot
string-array.item: On its own: ء
Sitting on an alif (أ إ), a wāw (ؤ) or a yāʾ (ئ).
The letter it sits on is not pronounced, only the hamza and its vowel.

string-array.name: lesson_hamza_how
string-array.item: A short catch in the throat, like the break in “uh-oh”.
Don’t skip it or blend it into the vowel before it: nabaʾi, not nabai.

resources.string: The alif with a small ṣād (ٱ) is only pronounced when you start reading from it. A hamza (ء أ إ) is always pronounced.

string-array.name: lesson_ta_marbuta_spot
string-array.item: At the end of a word, shaped like a ه with two dots on top: ة, or ـة when joined.
It only ever comes at the end of a word.

string-array.name: lesson_ta_marbuta_how
string-array.item: When you continue to the next word, read it as t with its vowel: ar-rājifatu.
When you stop on it, read it as h: ar-rājifah. In this example the ayah ends, so you stop.

string-array.name: lesson_shadda_spot
string-array.item: A small mark shaped like a w above the letter: بّ.
The letter’s vowel is written together with it: بَّ‎, بِّ‎, بُّ.

string-array.name: lesson_shadda_how
string-array.item: Say the letter twice: first closing the syllable, then again with its vowel: rab-bi.
You can feel the letter held a little longer than a single one.

resources.string: A sukūn only removes the vowel. A shadda doubles the letter: the first half has a sukūn, the second has the vowel.

string-array.name: lesson_dagger_alif_spot
string-array.item: A small upright alif above a letter, instead of a full alif after it: مَٰ.
Common in words such as ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ and ذَٰلِكَ.

string-array.name: lesson_dagger_alif_how
string-array.item: Read it exactly like a normal long ā: two counts.

resources.string: A full alif sits on the line after the letter; a dagger alif is small and above it. Both are the same long ā.

string-array.name: lesson_small_madd_spot
string-array.item: A small wāw or yāʾ after a letter, most often after the hāʾ that means “him” or “his”: بِهِۦ‎, لَهُۥ.
It is written small because it is not part of the basic spelling.

string-array.name: lesson_small_madd_how
string-array.item: Lengthen the vowel before it for two counts, like a normal long vowel: bihī, lahū.
When you stop on the word, leave it out: bih, lah.

resources.string: A full wāw or yāʾ is part of the spelling. A small one shows a long vowel that is read but not written in full.

string-array.name: lesson_hamzat_wasl_spot
string-array.item: An alif with a small ṣād on top (ٱ), at the start of a word.
Very common before the lām of “al-” (the).

string-array.name: lesson_hamzat_wasl_how
string-array.item: If you start reading from this word, say it as a short vowel: ihdinā, al-ḥamdu.
If you join it to the word before, skip it completely: …nastaʿīnu-hdinā.

resources.string: A hamza (ء أ إ) is always pronounced. The ٱ is silent when you join it to the word before.

string-array.name: lesson_silent_spot
string-array.item: A small circle above a letter: that letter is never read.
Most often the alif after the wāw at the end of a verb, as in قَالُواْ.
In أَنَا (anā, “I”) the last alif is only read when you stop on the word.

string-array.name: lesson_silent_how
string-array.item: Skip the letter completely, as if it were not written.

resources.string: A letter with sukūn is pronounced, just without a vowel. A small circle means the letter is not pronounced at all.

string-array.name: lesson_stop_signs_spot
string-array.item: Small letters above the end of a word. They are not part of the word.
صلى: you may stop, but it is better to continue. That is the sign in this example.
قلى: you may continue, but it is better to stop.
ج: stopping and continuing are both fine.
م: stop here.
Three dots appearing twice, close together: stop at one of the two places, not both.

string-array.name: lesson_stop_signs_how
string-array.item: When you stop, end the last word without its vowel.
Take a breath only where you stop, never in the middle of a word.

string-array.name: lesson_sajdah_spot
string-array.item: The ۩ sign at the end of an ayah.
There are 15 of these places in the Quran.

string-array.name: lesson_sajdah_how
string-array.item: Recite the ayah as usual.
It is the practice to make one prostration, sajdat al-tilāwa, after reciting it.

resources.string: Stop signs are about pausing your recitation. ۩ marks a place of prostration.

string-array.name: lesson_izhar_spot
string-array.item: A noon with a sukūn (نۡ), or tanwīn with its two marks stacked on top of each other.
The next letter is one of the six throat letters: ء ه ع ح غ خ.

string-array.name: lesson_izhar_how
string-array.item: Say the n clearly and move straight on to the throat letter.
No extra nasal hum, and don’t hide the n.

resources.string: In ikhfāʾ the n is hidden with a nasal hum. In iẓhār it is said clearly.

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_ghunnah_spot
string-array.item: A word ends with a noon that has no mark, or with tanwīn.
The next word starts with ي ن م or و.
It only happens between two words. Inside one word, as in دُنۡيَا, the noon stays clear.

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_ghunnah_how
string-array.item: Don’t say the n. Go into the next letter as if it were doubled.
Keep a nasal hum for two counts while you do: jaw-wah.

resources.string: Before ل or ر the noon also merges, but with no nasal hum.

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_no_ghunnah_spot
string-array.item: A word ends with a noon that has no mark, or with tanwīn.
The next word starts with ل or ر, and that letter has a shadda: لّ or رّ.

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_no_ghunnah_how
string-array.item: Drop the n sound completely.
Go straight into a doubled ل or ر, with no nasal hum.

resources.string: Before ي ن م و the noon merges too, but a nasal hum stays.

string-array.name: lesson_iqlab_spot
string-array.item: A small meem above the noon (نۢ), or in place of the second tanwīn mark.
The next letter is always ب.

string-array.name: lesson_iqlab_how
string-array.item: Turn the n into an m.
Close your lips lightly and hum for two counts, then say the ب.

resources.string: In ikhfāʾ shafawī the m is already written as a meem. In iqlāb a noon becomes one.

string-array.name: lesson_ikhfa_spot
string-array.item: A noon with no mark, or tanwīn with its two marks side by side, not stacked.
The next letter is one of the other fifteen: ت ث ج د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ف ق ك.

string-array.name: lesson_ikhfa_how
string-array.item: Don’t touch the n with your tongue. Hum through your nose for two counts instead.
Shape your mouth for the next letter while you hum.

resources.string: In iẓhār the n is said clearly, before the throat letters. In ikhfāʾ it is hidden.

string-array.name: lesson_izhar_shafawi_spot
string-array.item: A meem with a sukūn (مۡ).
The next letter is anything except ب or م.

string-array.name: lesson_izhar_shafawi_how
string-array.item: Close your lips and say a clear m, with no extra hum.
Take extra care before و and ف, where it is easy to blur the m.

resources.string: Iẓhār is the same idea for a noon: said clearly before a throat letter.

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_shafawi_spot
string-array.item: A word ends with a meem that has no mark.
The next word starts with a meem with a shadda (مّ).

string-array.name: lesson_idgham_shafawi_how
string-array.item: Join the two into one doubled m.
Hold it with a nasal hum for two counts.

resources.string: Idghām with ghunnah is the same merge for a noon, before ي ن م و.

string-array.name: lesson_ikhfa_shafawi_spot
string-array.item: A word ends with a meem that has no mark.
The next word starts with ب.

string-array.name: lesson_ikhfa_shafawi_how
string-array.item: Let your lips touch lightly, without pressing, and hum for two counts.
Then open into the ب.

resources.string: Iqlāb sounds the same, but there a noon or tanwīn turns into the meem.

string-array.name: lesson_heavy_letters_spot
string-array.item: Seven letters: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ. They are often remembered as the phrase خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ.
They are heavy wherever they appear, whatever their vowel.

string-array.name: lesson_heavy_letters_how
string-array.item: Raise the back of your tongue towards the roof of your mouth, so the sound is full and deep.
A fatḥa or alif after a heavy letter sounds deeper too: ṣā, not sā.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_jawf_spot
string-array.item: The long vowels: alif after a fatḥa, wāw after a ḍamma, yāʾ after a kasra, and the small alif, wāw and yāʾ.
They touch no part of the mouth: the sound flows from the empty space of the mouth and throat until the breath stops.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_jawf_how
string-array.item: Open the mouth for ā, round the lips for ū, spread them for ī, and let the voice run.
Hold each for two counts, so ʿā and mī in this word are longer than the short vowels around them.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_throat_spot
string-array.item: Six letters: ء and ه from the deepest part of the throat, ع and ح from the middle, غ and خ from the top, nearest the mouth.
A hamza on a seat (أ إ ؤ ئ) is a throat letter too.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_throat_how
string-array.item: Feel these in your throat, not your mouth.
ح is a breathy h with the middle of the throat narrowed; ع is the same place with the voice on.
Don’t soften ح into the ه of “hat”: they come from different parts of the throat.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_tongue_spot
string-array.item: Eighteen letters, from the back of the tongue to its tip: ق ك, then ج ش ي, ض, ل ن ر, ط د ت, ص س ز, and ظ ذ ث.
Yāʾ is a tongue letter when it has a vowel, sukūn or shadda; as a long ī it flows from the empty space.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_tongue_how
string-array.item: ق is made at the very back of the tongue, deeper than ك.
ت د ط touch the roots of the upper front teeth; ث ذ ظ touch the edges of the teeth with the tongue slightly out.
ض uses the side of the tongue against the upper back teeth.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_lips_spot
string-array.item: Four letters: ب, م and wāw with a vowel or sukūn use both lips; ف uses the lower lip and the upper teeth.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_lips_how
string-array.item: ب and م close the lips fully; و rounds them without closing.
For ف, rest the edges of the upper front teeth lightly on the inside of the lower lip.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_nose_spot
string-array.item: The ghunnah: the hum of noon and meem, heard most in نّ and مّ and wherever a noon or meem is hidden or merged.

string-array.name: lesson_makhraj_nose_how
string-array.item: Let the sound resonate in your nose for about two counts.
Pinch your nose: if the hum stops, it is coming from the right place.

resources.string: Ghunnah is the rule for when to hum; the nose is where the hum is made.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_shamsiyya_spot
string-array.item: After ال the lām has no mark, and the next letter has a shadda: ٱلرَّ.
The 14 sun letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_shamsiyya_how
string-array.item: Don’t say the lām.
Double the next letter instead: ar-raḥmān, ash-shams.

resources.string: Before a moon letter the lām has a sukūn and is said clearly: al-qamar.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_qamariyya_spot
string-array.item: After ال the lām has a sukūn: ٱلۡ.
The 14 moon letters are all in the phrase ٱبۡغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفۡ عَقِيمَهُ.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_qamariyya_how
string-array.item: Say the lām clearly, then the next letter: al-ḥamdu, al-qamar.

resources.string: Before a sun letter the lām is silent and the next letter is doubled: ash-shams.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_of_allah_spot
string-array.item: The doubled lām in the name ٱللَّه, also in لِلَّهِ and ٱللَّهُمَّ.
Look at the vowel just before it, even at the end of the word before.

string-array.name: lesson_lam_of_allah_how
string-array.item: After fatḥa or ḍamma, say the lām heavy: huwa-llāhu, qāla-llāhu.
After kasra, say it light: bismi-llāhi.

resources.string: The seven heavy letters are always heavy. The lām is normally light and is heavy only in the name Allāh after a or u.

string-array.name: lesson_ghunnah_spot
string-array.item: A noon or meem with a shadda: نّ or مّ.

string-array.name: lesson_ghunnah_how
string-array.item: Hold the n or m with a hum through your nose for two counts.
Try pinching your nose: if the sound stops, you are doing it right.

resources.string: Idghām with ghunnah creates the same hum when a noon merges into the next word.

string-array.name: lesson_qalqalah_spot
string-array.item: Five letters: ق ط ب ج د, remembered as قُطْبُ جَدٍّ.
They bounce when they have a sukūn, or when you stop on them, as at the end of this ayah.

string-array.name: lesson_qalqalah_how
string-array.item: Close on the letter, then release it with a small echo, without adding a vowel.
The echo is stronger when you stop on the letter than in the middle of a word.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_sign_spot
string-array.item: A wavy line over a long vowel: آ.
It is followed by a hamza, a sukūn or a shadda, which is why the vowel is stretched.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_sign_how
string-array.item: Stretch the vowel beyond two counts. How far depends on what follows: see the three kinds of madd.

resources.string: Without the wavy line a long vowel is only two counts.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_muttasil_spot
string-array.item: A long vowel with the madd sign, followed by a hamza in the same word: ـَآء.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_muttasil_how
string-array.item: Stretch it for 4 or 5 counts, the same length every time you recite.
It must always be stretched. Shortening it is a mistake.

resources.string: In munfaṣil the hamza starts the next word, not the same word.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_munfasil_spot
string-array.item: A word ends with a long vowel and the madd sign.
The next word starts with a hamza.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_munfasil_how
string-array.item: Stretch it for 4 or 5 counts, the same length as muttaṣil.
If you stop on the first word, it is a normal two-count vowel.

resources.string: In muttaṣil the hamza is in the same word.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_lazim_spot
string-array.item: A long vowel with the madd sign, followed in the same word by a shadda or a fixed sukūn.
It also appears in some of the letters that open surahs, such as الٓمٓ.

string-array.name: lesson_madd_lazim_how
string-array.item: Always stretch it for 6 counts.

resources.string: Muttaṣil is 4 to 5 counts and comes before a hamza. Lāzim is 6 counts and comes before a shadda or sukūn.
